claim: Mutations in the fukutin-related protein (FKRP) cause Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS), a severe form of congenital muscular dystrophy.
source: Mutations in the fukutin-related protein (FKRP) cause Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS), a severe form of congenital muscular dystrophy.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this relationship.

claim: A WWS human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived myogenic model recapitulates hallmarks of WWS pathology.
source: Here, we established a WWS human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived myogenic model that recapitulates hallmarks of WWS pathology.
evidence: The manuscript describes the establishment and characterization of this model with experimental data.

claim: Functional recovery of WWS myotubes is promoted by ribitol.
source: We show that functional recovery of WWS myotubes is promoted not only by ribitol but also by its precursor ribose.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing ribitol treatment rescues α-dystroglycan glycosylation.

claim: Functional recovery of WWS myotubes is promoted by ribose.
source: We show that functional recovery of WWS myotubes is promoted not only by ribitol but also by its precursor ribose.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing ribose treatment rescues α-dystroglycan glycosylation.

claim: The combination of ribitol with NAD+ results in a synergistic effect on rescue of α-dystroglycan glycosylation.
source: Moreover, we found that the combination of each of these metabolites with NAD+ results in a synergistic effect, as demonstrated by rescue of α-dystroglycan glycosylation and laminin binding capacity.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data comparing ribitol alone versus ribitol+NAD+ treatment.

claim: The combination of ribose with NAD+ results in a synergistic effect on rescue of α-dystroglycan glycosylation.
source: Moreover, we found that the combination of each of these metabolites with NAD+ results in a synergistic effect, as demonstrated by rescue of α-dystroglycan glycosylation and laminin binding capacity.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data comparing ribose alone versus ribose+NAD+ treatment.

claim: FKRP residual enzymatic capacity is required for rescue by ribitol and ribose.
source: Mechanistically, we found that FKRP residual enzymatic capacity, characteristic of many recessive FKRP mutations, is required for rescue as supported by functional and structural mutational analyses.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from FKRP knockout and C318Y mutant cells showing no rescue, along with structural analysis.

claim: Mutations in FKRP result in a broad spectrum of muscular dystrophy phenotypes, ranging from mild Limb-Girdle MD (LGMDR9) to Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS).
source: Mutations in the fukutin-related protein (FKRP) gene result in a broad spectrum of muscular dystrophy (MD) phenotypes, ranging from mild Limb-Girdle MD (LGMDR9) to Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS), the most severe form of congenital MD (CMD) (Beltran-Valero de Bernabé et al., 2004; Brockington et al., 2001a; Brockington et al., 2001b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The biochemical hallmark of FKRP muscle disorders is hypoglycosylation of α-dystroglycan (α-DG).
source: The biochemical hallmark of FKRP muscle disorders is hypoglycosylation of α-dystroglycan (α-DG), which leads to disruption in the interaction of α-DG with extracellular matrix proteins, in particular laminin-α2, which is essential for muscle fiber integrity (Ervasti and Campbell, 1993; Ibraghimov-Beskrovnaya et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hypoglycosylation of α-dystroglycan leads to disruption in the interaction of α-DG with extracellular matrix proteins, in particular laminin-α2.
source: The biochemical hallmark of FKRP muscle disorders is hypoglycosylation of α-dystroglycan (α-DG), which leads to disruption in the interaction of α-DG with extracellular matrix proteins, in particular laminin-α2, which is essential for muscle fiber integrity (Ervasti and Campbell, 1993; Ibraghimov-Beskrovnaya et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The interaction between α-DG and laminin-α2 is essential for muscle fiber integrity.
source: The biochemical hallmark of FKRP muscle disorders is hypoglycosylation of α-dystroglycan (α-DG), which leads to disruption in the interaction of α-DG with extracellular matrix proteins, in particular laminin-α2, which is essential for muscle fiber integrity (Ervasti and Campbell, 1993; Ibraghimov-Beskrovnaya et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: WWS has reduced life expectancy of less than 3 years.
source: Due to its rarity and reduced life expectancy (<3 years), disease pathogenesis and treatment strategies remain elusive for WWS.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about WWS.

claim: There is no effective treatment for FKRP-associated MDs.
source: To date, there is no effective treatment for FKRP-associated MDs (Ortiz-Cordero et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: FKRP is a ribitol-5-phosphate transferase.
source: FKRP is a ribitol-5-phosphate transferase, that in tandem with fukutin (FKTN), adds ribitol 5-phosphate onto the 3GalNAc-β1-3GlcNAc-β1–4(P-6) Man-1-Thr/Ser modification of α-DG (Core M3) (Manya et al., 2004; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013), using cytidine diphosphate (CDP)-ribitol, which is produced by isoprenoid synthase domain-containing protein (ISPD) (Gerin et al., 2016; Kanagawa et al., 2016; Praissman et al., 2016; Riemersma et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FKRP, in tandem with fukutin (FKTN), adds ribitol 5-phosphate onto the 3GalNAc-β1-3GlcNAc-β1–4(P-6) Man-1-Thr/Ser modification of α-DG (Core M3).
source: FKRP is a ribitol-5-phosphate transferase, that in tandem with fukutin (FKTN), adds ribitol 5-phosphate onto the 3GalNAc-β1-3GlcNAc-β1–4(P-6) Man-1-Thr/Ser modification of α-DG (Core M3) (Manya et al., 2004; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013), using cytidine diphosphate (CDP)-ribitol, which is produced by isoprenoid synthase domain-containing protein (ISPD) (Gerin et al., 2016; Kanagawa et al., 2016; Praissman et al., 2016; Riemersma et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FKRP uses cytidine diphosphate (CDP)-ribitol as a substrate.
source: FKRP is a ribitol-5-phosphate transferase, that in tandem with fukutin (FKTN), adds ribitol 5-phosphate onto the 3GalNAc-β1-3GlcNAc-β1–4(P-6) Man-1-Thr/Ser modification of α-DG (Core M3) (Manya et al., 2004; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013), using cytidine diphosphate (CDP)-ribitol, which is produced by isoprenoid synthase domain-containing protein (ISPD) (Gerin et al., 2016; Kanagawa et al., 2016; Praissman et al., 2016; Riemersma et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CDP-ribitol is produced by isoprenoid synthase domain-containing protein (ISPD).
source: FKRP is a ribitol-5-phosphate transferase, that in tandem with fukutin (FKTN), adds ribitol 5-phosphate onto the 3GalNAc-β1-3GlcNAc-β1–4(P-6) Man-1-Thr/Ser modification of α-DG (Core M3) (Manya et al., 2004; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013), using cytidine diphosphate (CDP)-ribitol, which is produced by isoprenoid synthase domain-containing protein (ISPD) (Gerin et al., 2016; Kanagawa et al., 2016; Praissman et al., 2016; Riemersma et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The presence of ribitol-5-phosphate is essential for the subsequent addition of −3Xylα1-3GlcAβ1 and (3Xylα1-3GlcAβ1)n-.
source: The presence of ribitol-5-phosphate is essential for the subsequent addition of −3Xylα1-3GlcAβ1 and (3Xylα1-3GlcAβ1)n- and, therefore, for allowing α-DG to bind to extracellular membrane ligands (Inamori et al., 2012; Manya et al., 2016; Praissman et al., 2014; Willer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ribitol-5-phosphate is essential for allowing α-DG to bind to extracellular membrane ligands.
source: The presence of ribitol-5-phosphate is essential for the subsequent addition of −3Xylα1-3GlcAβ1 and (3Xylα1-3GlcAβ1)n- and, therefore, for allowing α-DG to bind to extracellular membrane ligands (Inamori et al., 2012; Manya et al., 2016; Praissman et al., 2014; Willer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Addition of ribitol or ribose to fibroblasts from patients with ISPD mutations resulted in increased CDP-ribitol levels and rescue of α-DG functional glycosylation.
source: The addition of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) metabolites ribitol or ribose, a precursor of ribitol (Gerin et al., 2016; Huck et al., 2004), to fibroblasts from patients with ISPD mutations resulted in increased CDP-ribitol levels and rescue of α-DG functional glycosylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Rescue of α-DG functional glycosylation by ribitol or ribose varied significantly among samples with different mutations.
source: However, rescue varied significantly among samples with different mutations (Gerin et al., 2016; van Tol et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ribitol treatment in FKRP mutant mice modeling severe LGMDR9 partially restored α-DG functional glycosylation.
source: Cataldi et al., 2018 documented that ribitol treatment in FKRP mutant mice modeling severe LGMDR9 partially restored α-DG functional glycosylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Ribitol treatment of embryoid bodies from an LGMDR9 patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell line partly recovered the glycosylation defect.
source: More recently, Nickolls et al., 2020 showed that ribitol treatment of embryoid bodies from an LGMDR9 patient-specific induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell line partly recovered the glycosylation defect.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NAD forms (NAD+, NADH, NADP, and NADPH) are essential cofactors for oxidoreductases in the pentose phosphate pathway.
source: NAD forms (NAD+, NADH, NADP, and NADPH) are essential cofactors for oxidoreductases in the PPP (Singh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NAD+ supplementation in FKRP-deficient zebrafish led to decreased muscle degeneration and improved muscle function when administered at gastrulation.
source: Moreover, Bailey et al., 2019 reported that NAD+ supplementation in FKRP-deficient zebrafish led to decreased muscle degeneration and improved muscle function when administered at gastrulation, before muscle development occurs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: FP4 iPS cells were generated from a 1-year-old WWS male patient harboring two mutations in exon 4 of the FKRP gene: dc.558dupC (p.A187fs) and c.1418T>G(p.F473C).
source: Using an integration-free approach, we generated iPS cells from a 1-year-old WWS male patient (FP4) harboring two mutations in exon 4 of the FKRP gene, dc.558dupC (p.A187fs) and c.1418T>G(p.F473C) (Kava et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the generation of the cell line used in the study.

claim: FP4 iPS cells express pluripotency markers.
source: FP4 iPS cells express pluripotency markers, display normal karyotype, and develop teratomas containing cell types from all three germ layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: FP4 iPS cells display normal karyotype.
source: FP4 iPS cells express pluripotency markers, display normal karyotype, and develop teratomas containing cell types from all three germ layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cytogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: FP4 iPS cells develop teratomas containing cell types from all three germ layers.
source: FP4 iPS cells express pluripotency markers, display normal karyotype, and develop teratomas containing cell types from all three germ layers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by teratoma formation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: FP4 and control WT iPS cells show similar differentiation into MHC-positive myotubes.
source: Immunostaining for MHC showed similar differentiation between WT and mutant FP4 myotubes (Figure 1A, upper panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FP4 myotubes show drastically reduced IIH6 immunoreactivity.
source: Staining with IIH6, a monoclonal antibody specific to the laminin binding domain of α-DG (Ervasti and Campbell, 1993), showed drastically reduced IIH6 immunoreactivity in FP4 myotubes (Figure 1A, lower panel), which was corroborated by western blot.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and western blot data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: WWS FP4 myotubes show decreased molecular weight for α-DG core.
source: In accordance with the loss of α-DG functional glycosylation, WWS FP4 myotubes showed decreased molecular weight for α-DG core (Figure 1B), marked reduction in IIH6 (Figure 1B and C), and most importantly, lack of laminin binding, as demonstrated by the laminin overlay assay (LOA) following enrichment by wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) pull-down (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: WWS FP4 myotubes show marked reduction in IIH6.
source: In accordance with the loss of α-DG functional glycosylation, WWS FP4 myotubes showed decreased molecular weight for α-DG core (Figure 1B), marked reduction in IIH6 (Figure 1B and C), and most importantly, lack of laminin binding, as demonstrated by the laminin overlay assay (LOA) following enrichment by wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) pull-down (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: WWS FP4 myotubes lack laminin binding.
source: In accordance with the loss of α-DG functional glycosylation, WWS FP4 myotubes showed decreased molecular weight for α-DG core (Figure 1B), marked reduction in IIH6 (Figure 1B and C), and most importantly, lack of laminin binding, as demonstrated by the laminin overlay assay (LOA) following enrichment by wheat germ agglutinin (WGA) pull-down (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by laminin overlay assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Introduction of WT FKRP transgene into FP4 cells restores functional glycosylation of α-DG.
source: FKRP-overexpressing FP4 myogenic progenitors gave rise to MHC-positive myotubes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) that displayed increased FKRP expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and enhanced immunoreactivity to IIH6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and C), which led to rescue of laminin binding capacity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ribitol treatment at 50 mM concentration rescues α-DG functional glycosylation in FP4 myotubes.
source: Treated cells retained differentiation capacity, as shown by MHC levels (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and exhibited rescue of α-DG functional glycosylation (Figure 2B,C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and western blot data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claim: Ribitol treatment increases binding between α-DG and laminin in FP4 myotubes.
source: Importantly, this increase in functional glycosylation of α-DG was sufficient to increase binding between α-DG and laminin, as shown by the detection of laminin only in ribitol-treated FP4 myotubes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by laminin overlay assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ribose treatment at 10 mM concentration results in significant increase in functional glycosylation of α-DG in FP4 myotubes.
source: As shown in Figure 2E,F and G, we found a significant increase in functional glycosylation of α-DG upon 10 mM ribose supplementation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and western blot data shown in Figure 2E, F, and G.

claim: Ribose treatment enhances laminin binding capacity in FP4 myotubes.
source: This increase was sufficient to enhance laminin binding capacity in FP4 myotubes (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by laminin overlay assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Ribitol supplementation results in significant increases in ribitol, ribose, ribitol-5-P, and CDP-ribitol levels in FP4 myotubes.
source: The data from this analysis revealed that both ribitol and ribose supplementation result in significant increases in ribitol, ribose, ribitol-5-P, and CDP-ribitol compared to untreated cultures (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC/MS-MS data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ribose supplementation results in significant increases in ribitol, ribose, ribitol-5-P, and CDP-ribitol levels in FP4 myotubes.
source: The data from this analysis revealed that both ribitol and ribose supplementation result in significant increases in ribitol, ribose, ribitol-5-P, and CDP-ribitol compared to untreated cultures (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC/MS-MS data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sorbinil treatment results in decreased α-DG functional glycosylation in WT myotubes.
source: This resulted in a 40% reduction in IIH6 levels in WT myotubes (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Sorbinil treatment counteracts the positive effect of ribose on α-DG functional glycosylation in FP4 myotubes.
source: Most importantly, sorbinil treatment counteracted the positive effect of ribose in FP4 myotubes by 63%, as shown by the diminished rescue of IIH6 levels (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: NAD+ treatment alone results in a small, yet significant increase in functional glycosylation of α-DG in FP4 myotubes.
source: In FP4 myotubes treated with NAD+ alone, we observed a small, yet significant increase in functional glycosylation of α-DG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: NAD+ combined with ribitol results in a 59% increase in IIH6 positivity compared to ribitol alone in FP4 myotubes.
source: However, when we combined NAD+ supplementation with PPP metabolites, we observed, on average, a 59% increase in IIH6 positivity in ribitol/NAD+ when compared to ribitol alone (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: NAD+ combined with ribose results in a 50% increase in IIH6 levels compared to ribose alone in FP4 myotubes.
source: The same synergistic effect was observed when FP4 cells were treated with the NAD+/ribose combination, as levels of IIH6 increased on average 50% compared to ribose alone (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: The combination of NAD+ with ribitol or ribose promotes increased laminin binding capacity in FP4 myotubes.
source: Importantly, in both cases, the combination also promoted increased laminin binding capacity (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by laminin overlay assay data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Ribitol/NAD+ treatment on established myotubes led to an 85% increase in IIH6 immunoreactivity compared to ribitol alone.
source: Ribitol/NAD+ treatment led to an 85% increase in IIH6 immunoreactivity compared to ribitol alone (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Ribose/NAD+ treatment on established myotubes doubled functional glycosylation of α-DG at 48 hr compared to ribose alone.
source: Likewise, ribose/NAD+ treatment on average doubled functional glycosylation of α-DG at 48 hr when compared to ribose alone (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: NAD+ treatment leads to a small increase in ribose levels compared to untreated FP4 myotubes.
source: We found that NAD+ treatment led to a small increase in ribose levels compared to untreated counterparts, but no significant differences were detected in ribitol-5-P and CDP-ribitol, as shown by comparing untreated vs. NAD+, ribitol vs. ribitol/NAD+, and ribose vs. ribose/NAD+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC/MS-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: NAD+ treatment does not significantly affect ribitol-5-P and CDP-ribitol levels in FP4 myotubes.
source: We found that NAD+ treatment led to a small increase in ribose levels compared to untreated counterparts, but no significant differences were detected in ribitol-5-P and CDP-ribitol, as shown by comparing untreated vs. NAD+, ribitol vs. ribitol/NAD+, and ribose vs. ribose/NAD+ (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC/MS-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The synergistic effect of NAD+ is independent of the FKRP substrate CDP-ribitol.
source: These results suggest that the synergistic effect of NAD+ is independent of the FKRP substrate CDP-ribitol.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite quantification data showing no significant changes in CDP-ribitol with NAD+ treatment.

claim: FKRP KO myotubes lack functional glycosylation of α-DG.
source: Immunostaining for MHC showed similar differentiation between FKRP KO myotubes and respective control WT counterparts (Figure 5A), but as anticipated, FKRP KO myotubes lacked functional glycosylation of α-DG, as evidenced by immunostaining and western blot to IIH6 (Figure 5A and B) and absence of laminin binding (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining, western blot, and laminin overlay assay data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Treatment of FKRP KO myotubes with ribitol, ribose, or NAD+ does not rescue α-DG functional glycosylation.
source: Importantly, treatment of FKRP KO myotubes with ribitol, ribose, or NAD+ did not rescue α-DG functional glycosylation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: FKRP-C318Y myotubes display a similar phenotype to patient-specific FP4 myotubes.
source: Isogenic myotubes generated from FKRP-C318Y iPS cells displayed a similar phenotype to patient-specific FP4 myotubes (Figure 5D), thus confirming the in vitro WWS phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Ribitol, ribose, or combinations with NAD+ do not rescue α-DG functional glycosylation in FKRP-C318Y myotubes.
source: We tested ribitol, ribose, or combinations with NAD+ supplementation in cultures of FKRP-C318Y myotubes, as described above for FP4, and none of the metabolites were able to rescue α-DG functional glycosylation in these cells (Figure 5E), suggesting that rescue is mutation specific.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The C318Y mutation disrupts direct chelation to the Zn2+ ion in FKRP.
source: The C318Y mutation disrupts direct chelation to the Zn2+ ion and sterically hinders the binding site from occupancy.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the FKRP crystal structure.

claim: The C318Y mutation leads to significant, if not complete, loss of FKRP enzymatic function.
source: This result suggests that this mutation will lead to significant, if not complete, loss of enzymatic function, and therefore metabolite-mediated rescue is not possible.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis and experimental data showing no rescue.

claim: The F473C mutation results in a free energy change in substrate binding affinity of +4.3 kcal/mol.
source: The mutation of F473 to cysteine (F473C) present in the FP4 patient sample leads to a free energy change in substrate binding affinity of +4.3 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is based on molecular modeling calculations.

claim: The F473C mutation results in destabilization of the Michaelis complex formation with diminished enzyme efficiency.
source: This difference suggests that the F473C mutation results in destabilization of the Michaelis complex formation with diminished enzyme efficiency, and therefore, metabolite supplementation that increases CDP-ribitol levels allows for increased FKRP activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the free energy calculations and experimental rescue data.

claim: Functional FKRP is required for rescue of α-DG functional glycosylation by ribitol, ribose, and NAD+.
source: These results indicate that functional FKRP is required for rescue of α-DG functional glycosylation by ribitol, ribose, and NAD+.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data showing no rescue in FKRP KO and C318Y mutant cells.

claim: NAD+ can increase functional glycosylation of α-DG in a human WWS FKRP model.
source: We show for the first time that NAD+ can increase functional glycosylation of α-DG in a human WWS FKRP model, and when combined with ribitol or ribose, can significantly potentiate the rescue of the muscle pathology in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NAD+ promotes increased ADP-ribosylation of integrin receptors in zebrafish models.
source: Although the mechanism is not entirely elucidated, NAD+ was reported to promote increased ADP-ribosylation of integrin receptors, which in turn increase integrin and laminin binding, increase laminin-111 organization and subcellular localization of paxillin to cell adhesion complexes (Goody et al., 2012; Zolkiewska, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on zebrafish models.

claim: Overexpression of paxillin rescues muscle structure in dag1 but not in FKRP mutants.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of paxillin rescues muscle structure in dag1 but not in FKRP mutants, suggesting a different mechanism of action (Bailey et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NAD+ improved muscle function in Duchenne MD mouse models via reduced parylation, increased mitochondria function, and increased expression of structural proteins.
source: Previous studies in two Duchenne MD mouse models showed that NAD+ improved muscle function via reduced parylation, as well as increased mitochondria function and expression of structural proteins (Ryu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NAD+ treatment increases core α-DG levels in FKRP-C318Y myotubes.
source: Our data on the quantification of core α-DG in FKRP-C318Y myotubes that had been treated or not with NAD+ revealed a significant increase in core α-DG upon NAD+ treatment, whereas β-DG levels remained unchanged (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that NAD+ supplementation specifically increases α-DG.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: NAD+ supplementation specifically increases α-DG but not β-DG.
source: Our data on the quantification of core α-DG in FKRP-C318Y myotubes that had been treated or not with NAD+ revealed a significant increase in core α-DG upon NAD+ treatment, whereas β-DG levels remained unchanged (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that NAD+ supplementation specifically increases α-DG.
evidence: This is inferred from the western blot data showing differential effects on α-DG versus β-DG.

claim: The ability of PPP metabolites to partially rescue α-DG functional glycosylation is mutation dependent.
source: Our results suggest that the ability of PPP metabolites to partially rescue α-DG functional glycosylation is mutation dependent.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential rescue observed in FP4 versus FKRP KO and C318Y mutants.

claim: Phenotypes associated with mutations in the zinc finger loop region may not be rescued by ribitol and ribose.
source: Although further studies are required to determine which patients could benefit from this potential treatment, our results suggest that phenotypes associated with mutations in the zinc finger loop region may not be rescued by ribitol and ribose, whereas FKRP mutations in other regions of the catalytic domain are amenable to rescue, as shown for FP4.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and structural analysis.

claim: FKRP mutations in regions of the catalytic domain outside the zinc finger loop are amenable to rescue by ribitol and ribose.
source: Although further studies are required to determine which patients could benefit from this potential treatment, our results suggest that phenotypes associated with mutations in the zinc finger loop region may not be rescued by ribitol and ribose, whereas FKRP mutations in other regions of the catalytic domain are amenable to rescue, as shown for FP4.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the rescue observed in FP4 cells with the F473C mutation.

claim: Rescue of functional glycosylation of α-DG in ISPD fibroblasts was found to be mutation dependent.
source: This is in line with previous studies in ISPD fibroblasts, in which rescue of functional glycosylation of α-DG was found to be mutation dependent (Gerin et al., 2016; van Tol et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ribose is a commercially available supplement with no major side effects in humans.
source: On the other hand, ribose is a commercially available supplement, and to date, with no major side effects in humans (Dodd et al., 2004; Seifert et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on ribose safety.

claim: NAD+ levels can be increased by several vitamin B3 forms, such as nicotinic acid (niacin) and nicotinamide riboside.
source: Furthermore, NAD+ levels can be increased by several vitamin B3 forms, such as nicotinic acid (niacin) and nicotinamide riboside, which have been investigated, showing no major side effects (Elhassan et al., 2019; Guyton and Bays, 2007; Pirinen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Vitamin B3 forms that increase NAD+ levels have been investigated and show no major side effects.
source: Furthermore, NAD+ levels can be increased by several vitamin B3 forms, such as nicotinic acid (niacin) and nicotinamide riboside, which have been investigated, showing no major side effects (Elhassan et al., 2019; Guyton and Bays, 2007; Pirinen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on safety of vitamin B3 forms.

claim: IPS cell-derived myotubes serve as a reliable platform for in vitro disease modeling and drug screening.
source: Together, our results support the use of iPS cell-derived myotubes as a reliable platform for in vitro disease modeling and drug screening.
evidence: This is concluded from the successful use of the FP4 iPS cell-derived myotube model in this study.

claim: The data provide a rationale for the potential use of ribitol/NAD+ and ribose/NAD+ as therapeutics to increase α-DG functional glycosylation in patients with FKRP mutations.
source: Importantly, our data provide a rationale for the potential use of ribitol/NAD+ and ribose/NAD+ as therapeutics to increase α-DG functional glycosylation in patients with FKRP mutations.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data showing synergistic rescue effects.

claim: The null mutation for FKRP is embryonic lethal.
source: Because the null mutation for FKRP is embryonic lethal (Chan et al., 2010), most FKRP mutations are thought to have some residual activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Most FKRP mutations are thought to have some residual activity.
source: Because the null mutation for FKRP is embryonic lethal (Chan et al., 2010), most FKRP mutations are thought to have some residual activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that null mutations are lethal, so surviving patients must have some residual function.

claim: The zinc finger loop in the FKRP catalytic domain consists of four conserved cysteine residues (C289, C296, C317, C318) required for Zn2+ ion binding.
source: The zinc finger loop in the FKRP catalytic domain consists of four conserved cysteine residues (C289, C296, C317, C318) required for Zn2+ ion binding.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure analysis of FKRP.

claim: F473 makes up a small hydrophobic pocket with L348, I357, W359, V477, and P481 that is essential for CDP-ribitol substrate binding within the catalytic domain.
source: On the other hand, F473 makes up a small hydrophobic pocket with L348, I357, W359, V477, and P481 that is essential for CDP-ribitol substrate binding within the catalytic domain.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure analysis of FKRP.

claim: Metabolite supplementation that increases CDP-ribitol levels allows for increased FKRP activity in the F473C mutant.
source: This difference suggests that the F473C mutation results in destabilization of the Michaelis complex formation with diminished enzyme efficiency, and therefore, metabolite supplementation that increases CDP-ribitol levels allows for increased FKRP activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis and experimental rescue data.

claim: Ribose is a precursor of ribitol.
source: The addition of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) metabolites ribitol or ribose, a precursor of ribitol (Gerin et al., 2016; Huck et al., 2004), to fibroblasts from patients with ISPD mutations resulted in increased CDP-ribitol levels and rescue of α-DG functional glycosylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The reduction of ribose to ribitol is mediated by the sorbinil sensitive aldose reductase (AKR1B1).
source: The reduction of ribose to ribitol has been suggested to be mediated by the sorbinil sensitive aldose reductase (AKR1B1) (Gerin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: IIH6 is a monoclonal antibody specific to the laminin binding domain of α-DG.
source: Staining with IIH6, a monoclonal antibody specific to the laminin binding domain of α-DG (Ervasti and Campbell, 1993), showed drastically reduced IIH6 immunoreactivity in FP4 myotubes (Figure 1A, lower panel), which was corroborated by western blot.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: FP4 patient fibroblasts were obtained from a 1-year-old male patient.
source: FKRP mutant fibroblasts obtained from a 1-year-old male patient (Kava et al., 2013) were reprogrammed into iPS cells, named FP4, using the CytoTune-iPS 2.0 Sendai Reprogramming Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using feeder-free conditions, according to the manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: This describes the source of the patient cells used in the study.

claim: FP4 iPS cells were generated using an integration-free approach with the CytoTune-iPS 2.0 Sendai Reprogramming Kit.
source: FKRP mutant fibroblasts obtained from a 1-year-old male patient (Kava et al., 2013) were reprogrammed into iPS cells, named FP4, using the CytoTune-iPS 2.0 Sendai Reprogramming Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using feeder-free conditions, according to the manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the FP4 iPS cells.

claim: Ribitol treatment at concentrations higher than 50 mM did not improve rescue compared to 50 mM.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B
evidence: The figure shows that 50 mM ribitol was chosen for further studies, implying higher concentrations were not more effective.

claim: Ribose concentrations higher than 50 mM led to cell death.
source: Because the lowest concentration of ribose able to enhance α-DG functional glycosylation was 10 mM and higher concentrations led to cell death (>50 mM), we chose the concentration of 10 mM for further analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D to F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by phase contrast images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The 100 μM concentration of NAD+ was chosen based on previous documentation in the literature.
source: We treated FP4 cultures with 100 μM of NAD+, as this concentration has been previously documented (Goody et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.
